title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
content:
The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.
“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.
The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.
However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

report.summary: FAA expands its $875M AI advisory system SMART nationwide after a DC trial cut flight times and fuel use, though controllers' union says it was excluded.
report.background: The FAA has been under pressure to modernize US air traffic management as congestion, delays, fuel costs, and controller staffing strain the system. AI advisory tools are attractive because they can analyze large volumes of weather, traffic, and staffing data faster than manual processes. SMART was first deployed over Washington, DC, airspace in September, where the FAA says it helped reroute 180 flights and saved time and fuel. The agency now wants to scale those results to all 22 air route traffic control centers. The expansion also highlights a broader tension in safety-critical industries: agencies want AI efficiency, but labor groups and safety experts often demand involvement in design, testing, and validation.
key_points: The FAA is expanding SMART from the Washington, DC, region to all 22 US air route traffic control centers. The agency says the $875 million system rerouted 180 flights in its initial deployment, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight.

SMART is a cloud-based advisory tool that combines weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics. It predicts traffic patterns and recommends schedules, optimal routes, and arrival sequencing, but it does not directly control aircraft.

A human team of FAA specialists in DC validates SMART's recommendations before passing them to air traffic control facilities nationwide. This keeps a human-in-the-loop safeguard, though the exact validation process and error rates are not detailed.

Airlines support the rollout, but the union representing air traffic controllers says it was not involved in designing or testing the system. That dispute could affect trust, adoption, and future labor negotiations around AI in safety-critical operations.
report.impact: For the AI industry, SMART is a high-profile test of human-in-the-loop decision support in a safety-critical domain. Developers should watch how the FAA validates recommendations, measures error rates, and integrates AI with legacy air traffic systems. If successful, it could accelerate AI adoption in aviation logistics and public infrastructure, but failures or labor friction could slow similar projects. For airlines and passengers, the promise is fewer delays and lower fuel burn, though benefits depend on nationwide data quality and controller trust. For regular users, the system is mostly invisible: it may improve schedule reliability, but it also raises questions about accountability when AI advice influences safety decisions.
report.tools: To follow the space, watch the FAA's SMART documentation and safety case materials, the open-source BlueSky air traffic simulator for ATM research, the OpenSky Network for flight-tracking data, and NASA's air traffic management research. For developers, human-in-the-loop AI validation frameworks and explainable decision-support tooling are also relevant.
